marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q001.takeaway: The hard palate has keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, submucosa and posterior minor mucous glands.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q001.displayText: The hard palate contains keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, has a submucosa, and contains minor salivary glands. This keratinised stratified squamous epithelium has regional variations and may be orthokeratinised or parakeratinised (found in hard palate and gingiva). The bony structure of the hard palate is covered by a firmly attached mucosa in the central part. In the lateral parts, the hard palate also has a submucosal layer containing blood vessels. There are minor mucous-type salivary glands in the submucosa in the posterior part of the hard palate. Note: in orthokeratinized epithelium the cell nuclei disappear in the keratinized layer, whereas in parakeratinized epithelium flattened, highly condensed nuclei remain in the cell cytoplasm of the keratinized layer until exfoliation.

rationales.b: This option omits submucosa and minor salivary glands; posterior hard palate has a submucosal layer with minor mucous glands.
rationales.c: The hard-palate epithelium is keratinized stratified squamous, not non-keratinized.
rationales.d: This option incorrectly combines non-keratinized epithelium with absent submucosa; lateral hard palate has submucosa.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q002.takeaway: The gut muscularis externa normally has inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q002.displayText: The muscularis externa has inner circular muscle fibres and outer longitudinal muscle fibres. The gut wall receives its strength mainly from the muscularis externa, which is the thick layer of muscle surrounding the submucosa and is responsible for gut movements such as peristalsis. Notes: muscularis externa contains smooth muscle except in the upper part of the esophagus, where it has only striated muscle fibres. The stomach has three layers in the muscularis externa, with an extra oblique layer. In the colon, the outer longitudinal fibres join to form prominent bundles called the taenia coli. The source includes a labelled histological section of duodenum showing the inner and outer layers of muscularis externa.

rationales.a: This reverses the usual gut arrangement: circular muscle is inner and longitudinal muscle outer.
rationales.c: The muscularis externa has both circular and longitudinal layers, not circular fibers alone.
rationales.d: The muscularis externa has both circular and longitudinal layers, not longitudinal fibers alone.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q003.takeaway: The esophagus is covered mainly by adventitia; serosa is absent except on its short abdominal part.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q003.displayText: The serosa is absent in the esophagus and hence is not expected to be seen on microscopic examination. The esophagus has an adventitia made up of dense fibrous tissue covering the muscularis externa. Only the lower intra-abdominal part of the esophagus has a layer of peritoneal covering over it. The source additionally illustrates the general layers of the gut tube: mucosa (lining epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis externa (inner circular and outer longitudinal fibres), and the outer covering.
emphasis: serosa is absent in the esophagus

rationales.a: Mucosa is a normal component of the esophageal wall.
rationales.b: The muscularis propria/externa is a major esophageal wall layer.
rationales.c: Submucosa is present in the esophagus and contains compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q004.takeaway: The lower third of the esophagus contains smooth muscle only.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q004.displayText: The false statement is that the lower third of the esophagus contains only skeletal muscle. The lower third consists only of smooth muscle. The esophagus consists of mucosa with non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae; submucosa containing compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands; muscularis externa with the usual circular and longitudinal layers; upper one-third containing only skeletal muscle fibres; middle one-third containing both skeletal and smooth muscle fibres; lower one-third containing only smooth muscle fibres; and an adventitia composed of dense fibrous tissue. Only a short length of the lower esophagus has a peritoneal covering (serosa).
emphasis: lower third consists only of smooth muscle

rationales.a: The esophagus is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, so this is true.
rationales.b: The upper third contains skeletal muscle, so this is true.
rationales.c: The middle third contains both skeletal and smooth muscle, so this is true; smooth muscle alone is in the lower third.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q005.takeaway: Chief cells are concentrated in the basal/deep part of gastric glands.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q005.displayText: Chief cells are located mostly in the basal part of the gastric glands. Gastric glands are simple or branched tubular glands that lie perpendicular to the gastric mucosa. They can be identified in three main regions: basal/deep part, neck, and isthmus (which connects to the gastric pit). Chief cells, also called peptic or zymogen cells, are mostly found in the basal or deep portion of the gastric glands; they are cuboidal or low columnar, basophilic, contain prominent secretory granules, and secrete pepsinogen and lipase. Oxyntic/parietal cells are found in the upper part of the gland, are large and eosinophilic, and produce hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. Mucous neck cells are prominent at the neck and secrete mucus. Neuroendocrine cells lie mostly in the basal/deeper parts of glands and include G cells (gastrin), D cells (somatostatin), enterochromaffin cells (serotonin), ECL cells (histamine) and P/D1 cells (ghrelin). Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that multiply and replace other cells.

rationales.a: The gastric pit is the surface opening above the gland, not the chief-cell-rich basal region.
rationales.b: The isthmus connects the gastric pit to the gland and contains stem-cell activity; chief cells predominate deeper.
rationales.c: The neck contains mucous neck cells; chief cells are mostly in the gland base.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q006.takeaway: Pyloric glands are predominantly mucus-secreting, so many acid-secreting cells is the false statement.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q006.displayText: The pylorus consists mainly of mucus-secreting glands, so the statement that the pyloric antrum has many acid-secreting cells is false. Gastric glands are divided into principal/fundic glands in the body and fundus, cardiac gastric glands near the cardiac orifice, and pyloric gastric glands in the pyloric antrum. Principal glands contain chief cells, parietal cells, mucous neck cells, neuroendocrine cells and stem cells. Cardiac gastric glands are predominantly mucus secreting, though some parietal and chief cells are sparsely present. Pyloric glands predominantly contain mucus-secreting cells, along with neuroendocrine cells, especially gastrin-secreting G cells; parietal and chief cells are scarce.

rationales.b: Oxyntic (parietal) cells secrete hydrochloric acid; this statement is true.
rationales.c: Cardiac glands are predominantly mucus-secreting, so this statement is true.
rationales.d: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor as well as hydrochloric acid; this statement is true.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q007.takeaway: Brunner’s glands are submucosal glands of the upper duodenum.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q007.displayText: Brunner's glands (duodenal glands) are compound tubular submucosal glands present in the upper duodenum, above the sphincter of Oddi. The alveoli are lined mostly by mucus-secreting columnar cells. Their ducts pass through the muscularis mucosae and empty into the intestinal crypts of Lieberkühn. The duodenum can be differentiated from jejunum and ileum by these submucosal glands; jejunum and ileum do not have glands in their submucosa. The source shows a histological section of normal duodenum with Brunner's glands at the submucosal layer.

rationales.c: Brunner’s glands characterize the upper duodenum, not the lower duodenum as keyed here.
rationales.d: The appendix contains lymphoid tissue but not Brunner’s glands.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q008.takeaway: Peyer’s patches in the submucosa identify the ileum.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q008.displayText: The image is a section through the ileum, evident from thin and slender villi and an aggregated lymphatic follicle (Peyer's patch) in the submucosa. These aggregations of lymphatic follicles are known as mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), and also as gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT). Peyer's patches are found in large size and numerously in the terminal ileum.

rationales.a: The esophagus has stratified squamous lining and no ileal Peyer’s patches.
rationales.b: The stomach has gastric glands rather than ileal villi with Peyer’s patches.
rationales.d: Duodenum is identified by Brunner’s glands in its submucosa, rather than aggregated ileal Peyer’s patches.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q009.takeaway: Paneth cells are granule-rich; a foamy cytoplasm describes goblet cells, not Paneth cells.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q009.displayText: The foamy or frothy cytoplasmic appearance is not a feature of Paneth cells; it is a feature of Goblet cells. Mucus-secreting Goblet cells contain lipid or mucinous material with a foamy appearance. Paneth cells (enzyme cells) are present only in the deeper portions of the intestinal crypts. They contain many eosinophilic secretory granules, a significant amount of rough endoplasmic reticulum, and are rich in zinc. Their products include lysozyme, which kills bacteria, and other enzymes.

rationales.a: Paneth cells have abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum; this is true.
rationales.b: Paneth cells are rich in zinc; this is true.
rationales.c: Paneth cells contain lysozyme and other enzymes; this is true.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q010.takeaway: Neck cells are gastric gland cells and are absent from a duodenal section.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q010.displayText: Neck cells are not likely to be seen on microscopy because they are not present in the small intestine. Neck cells are mucus-secreting cells present in the upper end or neck of the main gastric glands of the stomach. Stem cells are undifferentiated cells present in the wall of intestinal crypts. Goblet cells are mucus-secreting cells with an expanded upper part distended with mucin granules and a flattened basal nucleus. Paneth (zymogen) cells are found only in the deeper parts of intestinal crypts and contain prominent eosinophilic secretory granules.

rationales.a: Stem cells are present in the intestinal crypt wall and can be seen in a duodenal biopsy.
rationales.b: Goblet cells are present in the small-intestinal epithelium.
rationales.c: Paneth cells occupy the deeper intestinal crypts; the absent cells are gastric neck cells.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q011.takeaway: Centroacinar cells are part of the intercalated ducts of the exocrine pancreas.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q011.displayText: Centroacinar cells are mainly present in the pancreas. They are present in the alveoli of the exocrine pancreas and are so named because they are visible near the centre of the acinus (or alveolus). These cells are actually part of the intercalated ducts that are invaginated into the secretory elements of the pancreas.

rationales.b: Parotid is a salivary gland; its secretory acini do not have centroacinar cells.
rationales.c: Prostate is not the site of centroacinar cells, which are pancreatic duct cells.
rationales.d: The liver has hepatocytes and bile duct structures, not centroacinar cells.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q012.takeaway: The portal triad contains portal-vein, hepatic-artery and bile-duct branches, not a hepatic vein.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q012.displayText: Hepatic vein does not form part of the portal triad. Portal canals are present at angular intervals at the periphery of each hepatic lobule and contain connective tissue. Each portal canal contains a branch of the portal vein, a branch of the hepatic artery and an interlobular bile duct; these three structures collectively form the portal triad. The source includes a cross-section of normal hepatic tissue illustrating the portal triad.

rationales.a: A hepatic-artery branch is one component of the portal triad.
rationales.c: An interlobular bile duct is one component of the portal triad.
rationales.d: A portal-vein branch is one component of the portal triad; hepatic venous blood drains centrally.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q013.takeaway: Kupffer cells lie on sinusoidal walls, not within the perisinusoidal space of Disse.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q013.displayText: The space of Disse contains the listed components except Kupffer cells. Kupffer cells, also called stellate macrophages or Kupffer-Browicz cells, are specialized macrophages present in the liver and are part of the mononuclear phagocyte system; they lie in the lining of the sinusoidal walls rather than in the space of Disse. The space of Disse, or perisinusoidal space, is between the hepatocyte and a sinusoid. It contains blood plasma. Microvilli of hepatocytes extend into the space, allowing absorption of proteins and other plasma components from sinusoids by hepatocytes. This space may also have some fat cells.

rationales.a: Hepatocyte microvilli extend into the space of Disse.
rationales.b: The perisinusoidal space contains blood plasma.
rationales.d: The source notes that some fat cells may be present in the space of Disse.

marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q015.takeaway: The membranous urethra is the listed exception to urothelial lining.
marrow__ANAT_CH15_Q015.displayText: Transitional epithelium lines all the listed structures except the membranous urethra. Transitional epithelium is found in the renal pelvis and calyces, ureter, urinary bladder, and pre-prostatic and prostatic parts of the urethra; because of this distribution, it is also called urothelium. Much of the urethra in both sexes is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium. The pre-prostatic and prostatic urethra have transitional epithelium, the membranous urethra is pseudostratified/stratified columnar, and the penile/spongy urethra is proximally pseudostratified columnar and distally stratified squamous.

rationales.a: Ureters are lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium).
rationales.b: Minor calyces are part of the urinary collecting system and are lined by urothelium.
rationales.c: The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium.
